title: Swedish Meatballs
subtitle: tender pork and beef meatballs in cream sauce
excerpt: Swedish meatballs are small, tender balls of pork and beef served in a rich cream sauce. They are eaten across Sweden as an everyday family meal. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Swedish meatballs have been a staple of Swedish home cooking for centuries. They became internationally known through IKEA's restaurants, which serve millions of portions each year.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the cooked meatballs without sauce for up to 3 months. Make the sauce fresh when reheating.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the meatball quantity and freeze half.

glossaryTerms.definition: Breadcrumbs soaked in liquid, added to mince to keep meatballs tender.

Combine the beef mince, pork mince, grated onion, egg and breadcrumbs in a bowl. Mix well, then roll into balls about 3 cm across. You should get around 24 meatballs.
Melt the butter in the large frying pan over medium-high heat. Fry the meatballs in batches, turning to brown all sides, about 8 minutes per batch. Transfer to a plate.
Pour the chicken stock into the same pan and scrape up the browned bits from the base. Bring to a simmer and reduce by one third.
Add the double cream and soy sauce. Simmer for 5 minutes until the sauce coats the back of a spoon.
Return the meatballs to the pan and heat through for 3 to 4 minutes. Serve immediately with mashed potato.

attrs.problem: The meatballs fall apart when frying.
attrs.solution: Chill the shaped meatballs for 20 minutes before frying. Make sure the pan is hot and the butter is sizzling before you add them.
Simmer the cream and stock for longer without the meatballs in the pan. It needs a few more minutes to reduce to a coating consistency.

attrs.problem: The meatballs are dense and tough.
attrs.solution: The mix was overworked. Mix just until combined and do not squeeze the mixture too hard when rolling.

content.text: Swedish meatballs appear on every Swedish smorgasbord and in homes across the country. They are served at Christmas julbord alongside pickled herring and potatoes. IKEA made them the most recognised Swedish food outside Scandinavia. At home they are a simple, comforting weeknight dish.
